Splendor vs Azul in 2026: Which One Is Right for You?

2026-10-07

Splendor vs Azul comes down to one question. Do you want to build quietly or fight in the open? Splendor is the quiet one. Azul is the sharp one. Both are 2 to 4 player abstract strategy games that finish in under an hour and cost under $35, and both have earned a permanent spot on my shelf.

I have owned both for years and played each more than fifty times. Here is the part most comparisons skip. These two games look like cousins on the shelf, and they attract completely different people. Buy the wrong one and it sits in shrink while the other table laughs. Buy the right one and you teach it to everyone you know.

Below is the honest breakdown. How each game actually feels, where each one wins, the one real flaw each has, and a third game to consider if neither clicks.

The Short Answer

If you want one line with no scrolling, here it is. Pick Splendor if your group likes calm, smart, low-conflict games that get faster the more you play them. Pick Azul if your group likes to needle each other, and you want a game that looks beautiful and cuts deep.

If you mostly play with two people, both shine, but Azul's two-player duel is the sharper version of either game. If you always have three or four at the table, Azul handles the bigger crowd better. Keep reading if you want the reasons, because the reasons are where the surprise is.

What Splendor Actually Is

Splendor is a game about buying gems with gems. On your turn you do exactly one thing. You take three gem tokens of different colors, take two tokens of the same color, reserve a card you want, or buy a card you can already afford. Development cards are mines, shops, and merchants. Each one you buy gives you a permanent discount on future cards and sometimes victory points.

That is the whole game. Your first turn you own nothing. Ten turns later you can afford almost anything, because every card you buy makes the next one cheaper. The first player to 15 points triggers the final round, and the nobles in the corner hand out bonus points if your gems match their taste.

Here is the key insight about Splendor. It is an engine builder wearing a trading game's clothes. The fun arrives the moment your discounts stack up and you start buying two cards a turn. My friend Tom lost his first eight games to me, borrowed my copy, studied the noble cards for a week, and now beats me more often than not. The game rewards planning, not luck.

The honest flaw? Splendor can feel like four people solving a puzzle next to each other. You mostly stare at your own board and grab what you need, and the interaction stays thin. Some nights that calm is exactly right. Some nights it falls flat. Full notes on the Splendor page.

What Azul Actually Is

Azul is a game about taking tiles your friends needed. On your turn you pick every tile of one color from a factory wheel or the center pile, then slide them onto one of the five rows on your board. Whatever you cannot place drops to the floor line and costs you points at the end of the round.

When a row fills, one tile moves over to the wall and scores. Placed tiles score more when they sit next to each other, so every position is a small math problem. The game ends when someone completes a horizontal row on the wall, and the end bonuses decide who wins.

Here is what makes Azul different. The tiles you leave behind are the whole point. If you scoop up the last red tiles and the next player has nowhere to put what remains, you have just handed them a pile of negative points and a bad round. Azul won the Spiel des Jahres in 2018, and the design earns it every time.

The honest flaw is that Azul asks more of you. I have watched brand new players freeze on their first turn because every choice carries a punishment. It is not a heavy game, but it is not as forgiving as Splendor either. See the Azul page if you want the stats, and my how to play Azul walkthrough if you want the rules and the leftover rule before your first game.

The Difference Nobody Mentions

I thought I understood these two games after a year of playing them. Then I noticed something that changed how I recommend them to people.

Here is the contradiction. Splendor looks like a race and plays like solitaire. Azul looks like a calm puzzle and plays like a knife fight. Every review tells you Splendor is the engine builder and Azul is the tile drafter. That is true, and it is useless, because it never tells you which one your group will actually replay.

Pay attention to this number: one. In Splendor you make one quiet decision per turn and then pass. In Azul, every tile you take is a small attack on the person who plays after you. That is the real difference between them. Splendor is a game you play next to people. Azul is a game you play against them.

Which One for Your Group

Here is the honest decision tree, not a sales pitch. Match your group to the pick.

Brand new to the hobby, or playing with non-gamers? Splendor. Fewer moving parts, no punishment for hesitating, and the moment it clicks lands fast. Competitive group that talks trash? Azul. The whole game is built on tension and denying the person next to you.

Mostly two players? Azul first if you want a tense duel, Splendor first if you want a relaxed puzzle. Four players every week? Azul. It stays snappy at four, while Splendor can drag when people overthink their one action.

Family with kids? Azul. It is rated 8 and up, and the bright tiles keep younger players locked in. Five or more at your table? Neither of these is the answer, since both cap at four. See the best games for 6 players for that crowd instead.

The Third Option: Sagrada

If you love Azul's drafting and want the dice version of it, get Sagrada. You draft colored dice instead of tiles and build a stained glass window on your own board, with restrictions on which colors fit where. Same take from a shared pool feeling, but with dice and a tighter puzzle underneath it.

Sagrada plays 1 to 4 in about 40 minutes and costs around $43. It is the game I reach for on the nights Azul starts to feel solved. Look at the Sagrada page before you commit.

The Shelf Test

Here is the Shelf Test. Would it survive 10 plays on a shelf that already holds 40 games? That is the only standard that matters. A game earns its spot by getting picked, not by being pretty or expensive.

Splendor survives on speed. It is the game I grab when we have 30 minutes and want zero drama, and it gets sharper the more you play it. Azul survives on tension. It is the game I grab when everyone wants to compete, and ten plays in you are still finding new ways to bury your neighbor.

Here is the part that matters. For a first buy, grab Splendor at about $25 if your group is new or prefers calm, or Azul at about $32 if your group likes a fight. Prices bounce, so catch Splendor under $23 and Azul under $28 and you have done well. Both are gateway games for a reason.
